name: Tweencore
summary: Tweencore describes the highly commercialized visual culture marketed to pre-adolescent girls largely between the late '90s to 2014.
description:
Tweencore describes the highly commercialized visual culture marketed to pre-adolescent girls largely between the late '90s to 2014. Unlike the broader demographic concept of "tweenhood," Tweencore refers to a cohesive set of maximalist design tropes found in North American suburban mall retailers of the era, most notably Justice (formerly Limited Too), Claire's, and Aeropostale's P.S. line. The aesthetic is characterized by a high-saturation color palette (typically consisting of rainbow, violet, and pink), the extensive use of "animal print" (specifically zebra and leopard print in unnatural colors like lime green or hot pink), and in its 2010s iterations, "random" humor motifs (such as mustaches, tacos, and slogan tees).

Visually, it acts as the "lite version" of McBling . It borrows the glitter, sequins, and consumerist themes of McBling and the layered neon accessories of Scene , but sanitizes them for a younger mainstream audience, replacing the subcultural or sexualized elements with a polished and commercial "girl power" image.
culturalContext: Key values (per the Aesthetics Wiki): Friendship, humor, "randomness", expression

visualDNA.colour: Hot pink, lime green, cyan, purple, zebra print (black/white)

fashion.Overview: Fashion was mainly inspired by the popular McBling and 2000s Preppy aesthetics of the time. More feminine styles had flowers, rainbow, butterflies and heart graphics and patterns alongside quotes. Less girly tweens wore Scene-influenced outfits, which combined bright colors with black.
